title: Revisiting radio synchrotron diagnostics in star-forming galaxies
comment: 19 pages, 14 figures. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: Radio continuum observations are widely used to study cosmic ray (CR) electron populations and transport processes in star-forming galaxies, but their interpretation relies on several simplifying assumptions. Here, we revisit three common assumptions: that some vertical radio profiles can be explained by CR advection alone, that radio spectra directly trace the galaxy-wide CR electron spectrum, and that bremsstrahlung and Coulomb losses are negligible for radio-emitting electrons. We model radio emission using time-dependent CR electron evolution in a magnetohydrodynamical simulation of an isolated Milky Way-mass galaxy. CR electron spectra are evolved self-consistently along Lagrangian tracer particles with the CREST framework, including injection at supernova remnants, advection with the gas, and spatially and temporally varying radiative losses. We compare these results to commonly adopted steady-state models. We find that advection-only transport in self-consistently driven galactic winds fails to reproduce the extended vertical radio intensity profiles observed in edge-on galaxies, despite reproducing the observed steepening of spectral indices with height. This is because slowly accelerating winds keep electrons in strong cooling environments for too long. Matching observed radio haloes with advection alone requires unrealistically high midplane wind velocities, implying that additional transport or re-acceleration processes are required. Although galaxy-integrated CR electron spectra at radio-emitting energies are similar across models, the resulting synchrotron spectra differ systematically because radio emission is biased toward young electrons in dense, strongly magnetised regions. Finally, we show that bremsstrahlung and Coulomb losses significantly shape radio spectra even when their loss rate is subdominant and therefore cannot be neglected.

AI.tldr: This paper reexamines common assumptions in modeling radio continuum emission from star-forming galaxies using self-consistent CR electron simulations, finding that advection-only transport cannot explain observed vertical radio profiles, that radio emission is biased toward young electrons in dense regions, and that bremsstrahlung/Coulomb losses significantly affect radio spectra even when subdominant.
AI.motivation: To critically reexamine three simplifying assumptions commonly used to interpret radio continuum observations of star-forming galaxies: that vertical radio profiles can be explained by CR advection alone, that radio spectra directly trace the galaxy-wide CR electron spectrum, and that bremsstrahlung and Coulomb losses are negligible for radio-emitting electrons.
AI.method: Time-dependent CR electron evolution modeled in a magnetohydrodynamical simulation of an isolated Milky Way-mass galaxy, using the CREST framework to evolve CR electron spectra along Lagrangian tracer particles with self-consistent injection at supernova remnants, advection with gas, and spatially/temporally varying radiative losses.
AI.result: Advection-only transport fails to reproduce observed extended vertical radio intensity profiles despite matching spectral index steepening; galaxy-integrated CR electron spectra are similar across models but synchrotron spectra differ due to bias toward young electrons in dense, magnetized regions; bremsstrahlung and Coulomb losses significantly shape radio spectra even when subdominant.
AI.conclusion: Advection alone cannot explain radio haloes without unrealistically high wind speeds, necessitating additional transport or re-acceleration; radio emission is biased and does not directly trace the galaxy-wide CR electron spectrum; bremsstrahlung and Coulomb losses cannot be neglected in modeling radio spectra.

title: Characterizing the GD-1 Stream with DESI DR2 Data: Thin Stream and Hot Cocoon
comment: 29 pages, 15 figures, 8 tables, submitted to ApJ, comments are welcome, associated data for all Tables is available on zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19258456) including a jupyter notebook tutorial, see paper for more details
summary: GD-1 is among the longest, coldest stellar streams in the Milky Way, making it an ideal target for probing dark matter substructure through dynamical heating. We present a catalog of 608 spectroscopically confirmed GD-1 members from the first three years of Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) observations. This constitutes the largest homogeneous spectroscopic sample of GD-1, doubling the number of members previously available only through heterogeneous compilations combining multiple surveys with different systematics. Using these data, we derive updated stream tracks in sky position, proper motion, and radial velocity that extend over $100^\circ$ of the stream. We apply a Gaussian mixture model to decompose the stream into a dynamically cold thin component ($σ_V = 2.49\pm 0.28$ km s$^{-1}$, width $= 0.23\pm0.01^\circ$) and a kinematically hot cocoon ($σ_V = 6.13\pm0.75$ km s$^{-1}$, width $= 2.18\pm0.17^\circ$). The cocoon contains $\sim30\%$ of members and its velocity dispersion is consistent with $\sim11$ Gyr of heating by cold dark matter subhalos. We also detect a large proper motion dispersion ($41.36\pm4.98$ km s$^{-1}$) along the stream direction in the cocoon component. This feature indicates a significant line-of-sight distance spread in the cocoon, and its origin will be further explored in a forthcoming paper. These measurements demonstrate the power of DESI spectroscopy for characterizing the multi-component phase-space structure of stellar streams and constraining small-scale dark matter substructure.

AI.tldr: Using 608 spectroscopically confirmed GD-1 stream members from DESI (doubling existing samples), we derive updated stream tracks over 100°, decompose the stream into a cold thin component (σ_V=2.49 km/s, width=0.23°) and a hot cocoon (σ_V=6.13 km/s, width=2.18°, ~30% of members), with the cocoon's velocity dispersion consistent with ~11 Gyr of heating by cold dark matter subhalos, plus a detected large proper motion dispersion indicating significant distance spread.
AI.motivation: GD-1 is one of the longest and coldest stellar streams in the Milky Way, making it an ideal probe for detecting dark matter substructure through dynamical heating signatures.
AI.method: We used 608 spectroscopically confirmed GD-1 members from the first three years of DESI observations, applied Gaussian mixture modeling to decompose the stream into two kinematic components, and derived updated stream tracks in sky position, proper motion, and radial velocity over 100°.
AI.result: We identified a cold thin component (σ_V=2.49±0.28 km/s, width=0.23±0.01°) and a hot cocoon (σ_V=6.13±0.75 km/s, width=2.18±0.17°) containing ~30% of members. The cocoon's velocity dispersion matches ~11 Gyr of CDM subhalo heating. A large proper motion dispersion (41.36±4.98 km/s) along the stream direction in the cocoon indicates significant line-of-sight distance spread.
AI.conclusion: DESI spectroscopy is powerful for characterizing multi-component phase-space structure of stellar streams and constraining small-scale dark matter substructure.

title: Light, heavy, primordial: exploring the diversity of black hole seeding and growth mechanisms in the JWST era
comment: Submitted to OJA; comments welcome
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a puzzling population of massive black holes in the first billion years, many of which are over-massive compared to their hosts (obese black holes), and reside in metal-poor hosts, posing a challenge for theoretical models at these early epochs. In this work, we compare the observational properties of astrophysically-seeded black holes using the DELPHI semi-analytic model and cosmologically-seeded primordial black holes (PBHs) using the PHANES analytic model. We explore the growth of light ($\sim 100 M_\odot$) and heavy ($\sim 10^{3-5}M_\odot$) seeds through mergers and accretion (both Eddington-limited and at super-Eddington rates) in the astrophysical scenario; PBHs (seeded between $10^{0.5-6}M_\odot$) only grow through accretion at sub-Eddington rates. Comparing to observables at $z \sim 5-10$, the only model that can be ruled out is the one where we allow Eddington-limited accretion onto light seeds. The observed high values of the black hole mass-stellar mass relation ($0.3-1$) can be reproduced by both PBHs and heavy seeds accreting at super-Eddington rates. However, only the PBH and Eddington-limited heavy seeding models can simultaneously reproduce the observed black hole masses (${\rm M_{bh}}$), stellar masses ($M_*$), and extremely low host metallicities ($Z \leq 0.01 Z_\odot$) inferred at $z \sim 7-10$. Crucially, we find PBHs show decrease in the black hole mass-stellar mass ratio with increasing halo mass at all redshifts, contrary to any astrophysical black hole model. Selecting systems at $z \sim 7$ with ${\rm M_{bh}}/M_* > 0.1$ and bolometric luminosities $\sim 10^{44-46} {\rm erg~s^{-1}}$ that show a negative black hole to stellar mass ratio and reside in $10^{9-11}M_\odot$ halos offer a promising clustering-based discriminant of PBH seeding models.

AI.tldr: This paper compares astrophysically-seeded black holes (DELPHI model) vs. primordial black holes (PBHs; PHANES model) to explain JWST's observed over-massive black holes in metal-poor hosts at z~5-10. Both PBHs and heavy super-Eddington seeds can reproduce the high Mbh/M* ratios (~0.3-1), but only PBHs and Eddington-limited heavy seeding match the extremely low metallicities (Z≤0.01 Z⊙). PBHs uniquely show a decreasing Mbh/M* ratio with increasing halo mass, offering a clustering-based observational discriminant.
AI.motivation: JWST has discovered a population of massive black holes in the first billion years that are over-massive relative to their host galaxies (obese black holes) and reside in metal-poor environments, challenging existing theoretical models of early black hole formation and growth.
AI.method: The authors compare two models: the DELPHI semi-analytic model for astrophysically-seeded black holes (light ~100 M⊙ seeds and heavy ~10^3-5 M⊙ seeds growing via mergers and accretion at Eddington-limited or super-Eddington rates) and the PHANES analytic model for cosmologically-seeded primordial black holes (PBHs seeded between 10^0.5-6 M⊙ growing only via sub-Eddington accretion). They compare model predictions to JWST observations at z~5-10.
AI.result: Only the Eddington-limited light seed model is ruled out by observations. Both PBHs and heavy super-Eddington seeds reproduce high Mbh/M* ratios (~0.3-1). However, only PBHs and Eddington-limited heavy seeding also match the extremely low host metallicities (Z≤0.01 Z⊙) at z~7-10. PBHs uniquely predict a decreasing Mbh/M* ratio with increasing halo mass at all redshifts, opposite to astrophysical models.
AI.conclusion: Observations at z~7 selecting systems with Mbh/M* > 0.1, bolometric luminosities ~10^44-46 erg s^-1, negative Mbh-M* ratio trend, and halo masses 10^9-11 M⊙ can serve as a clustering-based discriminant to identify PBH seeding models.

title: Interpretable Analytic Formulae for GWTC-4 Binary Black Hole Population Properties via Symbolic Regression
summary: Recent LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) analyses have revealed complex structure in the binary black hole (BBH) population, including distinct features in the primary mass spectrum and nontrivial spin-mass correlations. However, the phenomenological models used to capture these features often lack analytic transparency, making it difficult to isolate robust physical laws from modeling artifacts. To address this, symbolic regression is applied to the posterior inference products of the GWTC-4 catalog, discovering compact, closed-form analytic expressions for four key population relationships: (i) the merger-rate evolution with redshift; (ii) the mass-ratio dependence of the effective-spin distribution; (iii) the redshift evolution of the effective-spin distribution; and (iv) the conditional mass-ratio distributions associated with the 10 solar mass and 35 solar mass primary mass peaks. This framework successfully compresses both rigid and highly flexible models into differentiable phenomenological laws, dynamically recovering a consistent low-redshift merger-rate slope without assuming an a priori power-law form. The exact analytic derivatives provided by symbolic regression show that the mass ratio--effective spin and redshift--effective spin correlations are robustly driven by broadening of the posterior widths rather than shifts in the mean. Furthermore, qualitatively distinct functional forms for the mass-ratio distributions conditioned on the 10 solar mass and 35 solar mass primary mass peaks are identified. These closed-form expressions enable exact analytic gradient diagnostics and compact surrogate summaries, particularly for flexible numerical posteriors that are not otherwise available in low-dimensional analytic form. They also facilitate rapid downstream calculations for rate forecasting, formation channel comparison, and stochastic background estimation.

AI.tldr: Symbolic regression applied to LVK GWTC-4 data yields compact analytic expressions for BBH population properties (merger-rate evolution, spin-mass correlations, mass-ratio distributions), enabling exact gradient diagnostics and revealing that spin-mass correlations arise from posterior width broadening rather than mean shifts.
AI.motivation: Phenomenological models used to capture BBH population features lack analytic transparency, making it difficult to distinguish robust physical laws from modeling artifacts. Symbolic regression is applied to discover closed-form expressions for key population relationships.
AI.method: Symbolic regression applied to posterior inference products of the GWTC-4 catalog to discover compact, closed-form analytic expressions for four population relationships: merger-rate evolution with redshift, mass-ratio dependence of effective-spin distribution, redshift evolution of effective-spin distribution, and conditional mass-ratio distributions associated with primary mass peaks at 10 and 35 solar masses.
AI.result: The framework compresses rigid and flexible models into differentiable phenomenological laws, recovering a consistent low-redshift merger-rate slope without an a priori power-law form. Exact analytic derivatives show mass ratio--effective spin and redshift--effective spin correlations are driven by posterior width broadening, not mean shifts. Qualitatively distinct functional forms are found for mass-ratio distributions conditioned on the two primary mass peaks.
AI.conclusion: Closed-form expressions enable exact analytic gradient diagnostics, compact surrogate summaries for flexible numerical posteriors, and facilitate rapid downstream calculations for rate forecasting, formation channel comparison, and stochastic background estimation.

title: Chaotic migration of LISA Extreme Mass Ratio Inspirals in a turbulent accretion disk: effect on waveform de-phasing
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to ApJL. Comments welcome
summary: Gravitational wave (GW) detector LISA will observe near-coalescence extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs), which typically form in galactic central accretion disks. Gas torques on EMRI will alter its GW-driven inspiral trajectory from the vacuum expectation, leading to potentially LISA-observable GW dephasing ($Δψ_{\rm gas}$). Most studies compute $Δψ_{\rm gas}$ for a thin, laminar disk, with negligible flow turbulence, where the disk exerts a fairly well-understood linear torque ($T_{\rm lin}$). However, these disks must be turbulent due to magneto-rotational instability in the inner regions. Hence, we present a proof-of-concept general, agnostic prescription for the turbulent torque ($T_{\rm turb}$) acting on an EMRI by modeling it as a Gaussian distribution around $T_{\rm lin}$, based on recent advances from a global hydrodynamical (HD) study. We compute $Δψ_{\rm gas}$ for the ``golden'' circular EMRI with total source mass $M=10^6~{\rm M}_\odot$ and mass ratio $q=5\times10^{-5}$ in its final four-year evolution at redshift $z=0.276$ and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) $=50$ by varying Eddington ratio ${\rm f}_{\rm Edd}$, turbulence normalization $C$ ($=~360$ in the aforementioned HD study), disk aspect ratio $h_0$, and turbo-viscous coefficient $α$ in a reasonable parameters space. We find that for ${\rm f}_{\rm Edd}\gtrsim0.3$, $C\gtrsim300$, $h_0\gtrsim0.03$, and $α\gtrsim0.1$, gas-induced dephasings are unobservable if only considering $T_{\rm lin}$ but could become detectable ($Δψ_{\rm gas}>8/$SNR) if EMRIs exhibit chaotic migration due to turbulent gas flow. Hence, this work motivates running MHD simulations of accretion disks with embedded LISA EMRIs in the early in-spiral phase over long enough timescales to understand the evolution of their orbital elements and the imprint of the turbulent environment on their gravitational waveforms.

AI.tldr: Gas turbulence in accretion disks around supermassive black holes can cause detectable dephasing in LISA's gravitational wave observations of extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs), even when laminar gas torques alone would produce no observable effect.
AI.motivation: Previous studies of gas-induced GW dephasing for EMRIs assumed thin, laminar disks with linear torques, but inner accretion disks are inherently turbulent due to magneto-rotational instability. The impact of realistic turbulent torques on LISA-observable GW signals was unknown.
AI.method: The authors model turbulent torque as a Gaussian distribution around the linear torque, based on a recent global hydrodynamical study. They compute GW dephasing for a "golden" circular EMRI (M=10⁶ M☉, q=5×10⁻⁵, z=0.276, SNR=50) over its final four years, varying Eddington ratio, turbulence normalization C, disk aspect ratio h₀, and α-viscosity.
AI.result: For f_Edd≳0.3, C≳300, h₀≳0.03, and α≳0.1, gas-induced dephasings are unobservable under linear torque alone but become detectable (Δψ_gas > 8/SNR) when chaotic migration due to turbulent gas flow is included.
AI.conclusion: This motivates running long-timescale MHD simulations of accretion disks with embedded LISA EMRIs to understand orbital evolution and the imprint of turbulence on gravitational waveforms.

title: Relativistic effects in k-essence
comment: 21 pages, 12 figures
summary: Relativistic effects are sensitive to subtle changes in dark energy. These effects grow on very large scales and at high redshifts, which will be the reach of upcoming surveys. We investigate these effects in both the linear and the angular galaxy power spectra in a late-time universe dominated by cold dark matter and k-essence, focusing on three core models (dilaton, tachyon, and DBI scalar fields) and contrasting their predictions with those of the concordance model. By enforcing identical present-day cosmological parameters, we isolate the imprints of k-essence dynamics and perturbations on very large scales. We found that relativistic corrections dominate on very large scales and grow with redshift, but are largely insensitive to k-essence microphysics in Fourier space, leading to strong degeneracies among the models. However, in the angular power spectrum, where line-of-sight integrals are naturally included, relativistic effects are significantly amplified, yielding better sensitivity to clustering k-essence. In particular, the tachyon exhibits clear deviations across multipoles and redshifts, with distinct imprints in the Doppler and the combined (velocity and gravitational) potentials contributions. Furthermore, our results show that neglecting relativistic corrections can lead to systematic misestimation of deviations of k-essence from the cosmological constant. Our results show the relativistic angular galaxy power spectrum as a more consistent and robust probe of ultra-large-scale physics. These findings underscore the need for full relativistic modelling in next-generation surveys that are targeting horizon-scale modes, where the imprint of non-standard dark energy is most pronounced.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates relativistic effects in galaxy power spectra (linear and angular) for k-essence dark energy models (dilaton, tachyon, DBI), finding that relativistic corrections dominate on very large scales and are largely degenerate in Fourier space, but the angular power spectrum significantly amplifies sensitivity to k-essence dynamics—especially for the tachyon model—making it a robust probe of ultra-large-scale physics for next-generation surveys.
AI.motivation: Relativistic effects are sensitive to subtle changes in dark energy on very large scales and at high redshifts, which will be accessible to upcoming surveys. The study aims to investigate whether these effects can distinguish between different k-essence dark energy models and the concordance ΛCDM model.
AI.method: The authors investigate both linear and angular galaxy power spectra in a late-time universe dominated by cold dark matter and k-essence, focusing on three core models (dilaton, tachyon, and DBI scalar fields). They enforce identical present-day cosmological parameters to isolate k-essence dynamics and perturbations on very large scales.
AI.result: Relativistic corrections dominate on very large scales and grow with redshift but are largely insensitive to k-essence microphysics in Fourier space, leading to strong degeneracies. In the angular power spectrum, relativistic effects are significantly amplified, yielding better sensitivity. The tachyon model exhibits clear deviations across multipoles and redshifts, with distinct imprints in Doppler and combined velocity-gravitational potentials contributions.
AI.conclusion: Neglecting relativistic corrections can lead to systematic misestimation of k-essence deviations from ΛCDM. The relativistic angular galaxy power spectrum is a more consistent and robust probe of ultra-large-scale physics. Full relativistic modelling is needed in next-generation surveys targeting horizon-scale modes where non-standard dark energy imprints are most pronounced.

title: Cosmological Gravitational Waves from Ultralight Vector Dark Matter
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures
summary: We compute the abundance of cosmological gravitational waves produced during the evolution of an ultralight vector (spin-1) dark matter field. A homogeneous background vector field breaks spatial isotropy, requiring a Bianchi I geometry and inducing a mixing between the scalar, vector, and tensor perturbation sectors. We derive the perturbation equations in this background and show that, as a consequence of this mixing, scalar perturbations act as a source of tensor modes, generating a stochastic GW background. The production and cosmological evolution of these gravitational waves are implemented in a modified version of CLASS, from which we obtain the present-day spectrum.

AI.tldr: This paper calculates the stochastic gravitational wave background generated by an ultralight vector dark matter field, deriving perturbation equations in a Bianchi I geometry and implementing them in a modified CLASS code to obtain the present-day spectrum.
AI.motivation: To understand gravitational wave production from ultralight vector dark matter, which breaks spatial isotropy and requires a Bianchi I geometry, and to compute its present-day observational signature.
AI.method: Derive perturbation equations for a homogeneous vector dark matter background in Bianchi I geometry, accounting for scalar-vector-tensor mixing; implement the dynamical system in a modified version of the CLASS Boltzmann code to evolve perturbations and compute the GW spectrum.
AI.result: Scalar perturbations mix with tensor modes due to the anisotropic background, sourcing a stochastic gravitational wave background whose present-day spectrum is computed.
AI.conclusion: Ultralight vector dark matter produces a stochastic GW background via scalar-tensor mixing in anisotropic Bianchi I spacetimes, with the spectrum obtainable from modified CLASS simulations.

title: Constraining Dark Matter Density Profiles in UFDs with Wide Binaries: Forecast for the Chinese Space Station Survey Telescope
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 1 table, accepted for publication on MNRAS
summary: The internal structure of dark matter halos on sub-galactic scales remains a key open question, particularly in the context of the core-cusp problem. Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs), owing to their extreme dark matter dominance, provide a promising laboratory to probe these density profiles through stellar tracers. In this work, we assess the capability of the Chinese Space Station Telescope (CSST) to detect and characterize wide binary stars in the nearby UFD Segue 1, using mock observations. We generate mock binary populations based on our existing $N$-body simulations and incorporate realistic CSST observational conditions, including the expected deep-field limiting magnitude ($g \sim 27.5$ mag) and a photometric completeness of approximately $90\%$. The two-point correlation function (2PCF) of stellar pairs is used as a statistical tool to recover the binary fraction under these assumptions. We find that CSST can robustly detect wide binaries at the $3σ$ level for binary fractions as low as $f_b \gtrsim 0.01$, provided a stellar sample size of $N_{\mathrm{star}} \gtrsim 2300$. However, distinguishing between cusped and cored dark matter profiles is significantly more demanding, requiring $N_{\mathrm{star}} \gtrsim 6000$ and $f_b \gtrsim 0.1$ within $\sim 40\mathrm{kpc}$.

AI.tldr: This paper assesses the ability of the Chinese Space Station Telescope (CSST) to detect and characterize wide binary stars in the ultra-faint dwarf galaxy Segue 1, using mock observations. CSST can detect wide binaries at 3σ for binary fractions ≥0.01 with ≥2300 stars, but distinguishing cusped from cored dark matter profiles requires ≥6000 stars and binary fraction ≥0.1 within ~40 kpc.
AI.motivation: The internal structure of dark matter halos on sub-galactic scales, specifically the core-cusp problem, remains a key open question. Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs) provide an ideal laboratory to probe dark matter density profiles through stellar tracers, motivating the need to assess observational capabilities.
AI.method: Mock binary populations were generated from N-body simulations. Realistic CSST observational conditions (deep-field limiting magnitude g~27.5 mag, ~90% photometric completeness) were incorporated. The two-point correlation function (2PCF) of stellar pairs was used as a statistical tool to recover binary fractions.
AI.result: CSST can robustly detect wide binaries at the 3σ level for binary fractions as low as f_b ≥ 0.01, requiring N_star ≥ 2300. Distinguishing cusped vs. cored dark matter profiles requires N_star ≥ 6000 and f_b ≥ 0.1 within ~40 kpc.
AI.conclusion: CSST observations of Segue 1 can detect wide binaries and potentially probe dark matter profiles, but differentiating between cusp and core profiles demands significantly larger stellar samples and higher binary fractions than simple detection.

title: Impact of the Infrared Cutoff on Structure Formation in Tsallis Holographic Dark Energy
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. Comments, especially pointing out missing citations, are welcome
summary: We investigate the viability of Tsallis holographic dark energy (THDE) models, focusing on the role of the infrared (IR) cutoff in the growth of cosmic structures. Considering two commonly used choices of the cutoff, the particle horizon and the future event horizon, we analyze the evolution of linear matter perturbations and compute the growth factor, growth rate, and the observable $fσ_8(z)$. These predictions are compared with observational data from redshift-space distortion measurements. We find that the growth history is highly sensitive to the choice of IR cutoff. Models based on the future event horizon are consistent with observational data and can provide a fit comparable to, or slightly better than, the $Λ$CDM model for suitable values of the Tsallis parameter $δ$. In contrast, models constructed using the particle horizon generally fail to reproduce the observed growth of structure. These results demonstrate that the viability of THDE models depends crucially on the choice of IR cutoff and highlight the importance of structure formation as a stringent test of generalized holographic dark energy scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper tests Tsallis holographic dark energy (THDE) models by analyzing structure growth (growth factor, growth rate, fσ₈(z)) and comparing to redshift-space distortion data. Models using the future event horizon as IR cutoff fit the data comparably to or better than ΛCDM, while those using the particle horizon fail to reproduce observed structure growth.
AI.motivation: To assess the viability of THDE models by testing their predictions for cosmic structure formation, as a stringent test beyond background cosmology.
AI.method: Analyzed linear matter perturbations for two IR cutoff choices (particle horizon and future event horizon); computed growth factor, growth rate, and fσ₈(z); compared with observational data from redshift-space distortion measurements.
AI.result: THDE with future event horizon is consistent with data and can match or slightly outperform ΛCDM for suitable δ values; THDE with particle horizon fails to reproduce observed structure growth.
AI.conclusion: The viability of THDE models depends critically on the choice of IR cutoff, and structure formation provides a powerful discriminant for generalized holographic dark energy models.

title: Orbital evolution of highly eccentric bodies embedded in a ringed accretion disc
comment: 16 pages, 19 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Various processes can induce long-lived overdense rings and arcs in protoplanetary and AGN accretion discs, such as the accumulation of gas at the outer edge of the dead zone, or the infall of material. Using the local approximation of dynamical friction, we investigate the orbital evolution of a low-mass highly-eccentric point-mass accretor (perturber) embedded in an isothermal disc hosting a density ring. We specifically consider the regime in which the eccentricity exceeds four times the disc aspect ratio. For prograde perturbers, orbits that cross the ring progressively circularize while their semi-major axes converge toward the ring radius. As a result, perturbers accumulate, forming a population ring superimposed on the gaseous ring. The ring therefore acts as a migration trap for these eccentric orbits. We also find that prograde orbits tangent to the ring, either at apocentre or pericentre, remain tangential throughout their evolution; perturbers confined to these trajectories experience the highest accretion rates. In contrast, retrograde perturbers always migrate inward. Once the semi-major axis becomes smaller than the ring radius, the eccentricity grows, but not enough for the orbit to intersect the ring again. We also discuss how feedback effects, such as jet launching and thermal torques, could modify the effective forces acting on the perturbers.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the orbital evolution of low-mass, highly-eccentric point-mass objects (perturbers) crossing a density ring in isothermal protoplanetary or AGN accretion discs. Using a local dynamical friction approximation, the authors find that prograde perturbers circularize and accumulate at the ring radius (migration trap), while retrograde perturbers always migrate inward. Prograde orbits tangent to the ring remain tangential and experience the highest accretion rates.
AI.motivation: To understand how long-lived overdense rings and arcs in protoplanetary and AGN accretion discs affect the orbital evolution and accumulation of embedded eccentric perturbers, such as planetesimals or stellar-mass objects.
AI.method: The study employs a local approximation of dynamical friction to model the orbital evolution of a low-mass, highly-eccentric point-mass perturber embedded in an isothermal disc that hosts a density ring, focusing on the regime where eccentricity exceeds four times the disc aspect ratio.
AI.result: Prograde perturbers crossing the ring undergo progressive circularization and semi-major axis convergence toward the ring radius, leading to accumulation into a population ring. Prograde tangent orbits (at apocentre or pericentre) remain tangential throughout evolution and yield the highest accretion rates. Retrograde perturbers always migrate inward, and once their semi-major axis falls below the ring radius, eccentricity grows but insufficiently for re-intersecting the ring.
AI.conclusion: The density ring acts as a migration trap for eccentric prograde perturbers, potentially explaining observed accumulation patterns. Feedback effects such as jet launching and thermal torques may modify the effective forces and warrant further study.

title: Cosmological discrete self-similarity in primordial black hole formation
comment: 10 pages, 9 figures. Comments are welcome
summary: We demonstrate that discrete self-similarity (DSS), originally discovered in the collapse of a massless scalar field in an asymptotically flat system, survives in primordial black hole (PBH) formation within an expanding cosmological background. Using fully relativistic numerical simulations of massless scalar-field collapse in an Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker universe, we resolve the critical regime down to $|p-p_c|\sim 10^{-8}$, where $p$ and $p_c$ respectively are a parameter of the family of initial data and its threshold value, and find clear log-periodic oscillations in the PBH mass scaling relation. The detailed structure of these oscillations differs from that previously reported in the asymptotically flat case, exhibiting a more pronounced asymmetry between peaks and troughs. Analyzing two distinct families of initial data (Gaussian and piecewise rational curvature profiles), we find critical exponents and DSS periods that differ slightly but are broadly consistent within uncertainties. The presence of DSS implies characteristic log-periodic modulations in the PBH mass spectrum, with potential consequences for PBH abundances and the spectrum of induced gravitational waves.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that discrete self-similarity (DSS) exists in primordial black hole (PBH) formation within an expanding cosmological background, resolving down to |p-p_c| ~ 10^{-8} and finding clear log-periodic oscillations in PBH mass scaling, with implications for PBH abundances and induced gravitational waves.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether discrete self-similarity (DSS), previously known in asymptotically flat scalar-field collapse, also appears in primordial black hole formation within an expanding cosmological (FLRW) universe.
AI.method: Fully relativistic numerical simulations of massless scalar-field collapse in an FLRW universe, resolving the critical regime down to |p-p_c| ~ 10^{-8}, using two families of initial data (Gaussian and piecewise rational curvature profiles).
AI.result: Clear log-periodic oscillations in the PBH mass scaling relation are found; DSS periods and critical exponents differ slightly between initial data families but are broadly consistent. The oscillation asymmetry (peaks vs. troughs) is more pronounced than in the asymptotically flat case.
AI.conclusion: DSS survives in PBH formation in an expanding background, implying characteristic log-periodic modulations in the PBH mass spectrum, with potential consequences for PBH abundances and the spectrum of induced gravitational waves.

title: Early metal-enriched baryon cycling before the midpoint of cosmic reionization
comment: To be resubmitted after revision; Nature Astronomy
summary: Models predict that chemical enrichment and gas redistribution should proceed rapidly once star formation begins, yet direct observational constraints at the earliest cosmic epochs have been scarce. Here we present evidence that metal-enriched gas in multiple ionic phases was already present around galaxies before the midpoint of cosmic reionization. Using JWST/NIRSpec rest-frame ultraviolet spectroscopy of three galaxies at redshifts $z=7.2-9.3$, we detect blueshifted metal absorption in all three systems; across the sample, the detected transitions span neutral, low-ionization, and high-ionization species, including O I, Si II, C II, Si IV, and C IV. These absorption features show velocity offsets of order $|Δv| \sim 50$--$250\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, predominantly blueshifted relative to the systemic redshifts of the host galaxies derived from nebular emission lines. This ionic coexistence within a broadly shared velocity structure, together with the observed equivalent-width ratios, is consistent with outflowing or otherwise kinematically disturbed galaxy-associated gas, similar to that seen at lower redshift. The observations therefore indicate that metal-enriched gas associated with galaxies was already kinematically disturbed at very early times, requiring rapid metal production in the early generations of stars. These results show that key conditions for baryon cycling were established in at least a subset of luminous galaxies within the first several hundred million years of cosmic time, well before the completion of reionization.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRSpec observations of three galaxies at z=7.2-9.3 reveal blueshifted metal absorption in multiple ionic phases (neutral, low-ionization, high-ionization), indicating that metal-enriched, kinematically disturbed gas was already present around galaxies before the midpoint of cosmic reionization, requiring rapid metal production from early stars.
AI.motivation: Models predict rapid chemical enrichment and gas redistribution after star formation begins, but direct observational constraints at the earliest cosmic epochs (before the midpoint of reionization) have been scarce.
AI.method: JWST/NIRSpec rest-frame ultraviolet spectroscopy of three galaxies at redshifts z=7.2-9.3, detecting blueshifted metal absorption across neutral (O I), low-ionization (Si II, C II), and high-ionization (Si IV, C IV) species, with velocity offsets |Δv| ~ 50-250 km/s relative to systemic redshifts from nebular emission lines.
AI.result: All three systems show blueshifted metal absorption in multiple ionic phases coexisting within a broadly shared velocity structure. The equivalent-width ratios are consistent with outflowing or kinematically disturbed galaxy-associated gas, similar to lower-redshift analogs.
AI.conclusion: Metal-enriched gas associated with galaxies was already kinematically disturbed at very early times (first several hundred million years), requiring rapid metal production in early stellar generations and indicating that key conditions for baryon cycling were established well before the completion of reionization.

title: Aspects of gravitational clustering and structure formation in the Universe
comment: PhD Thesis
summary: The distribution of galaxies, halo abundance, and peculiar velocities are influenced by non-linear gravitational interactions, making the study of non-linear evolution crucial for accurate cosmological predictions. We explore these aspects using N-body simulations. Theoretical models of the halo mass function (HMF) can be formulated without referencing a cosmological model or input power spectrum. HMF obtained from N-body simulations show systematic deviations of 5-20\% from theoretical predictions. The physical origin of deviations may result from cosmology, the power spectrum, or both. We examine HMF deviations from universality for scale-free power spectra with an Einstein-de Sitter cosmology. We demonstrate that the mass function exhibits an explicit dependence on the slope of the input power spectrum. We find that an effective index of the $Λ$CDM model can correspond to the HMF from scale-free cosmologies as a first approximation. Furthermore, structure formation has led to deviations from homogeneity and isotropy on scales up to at least $100$ Mpc/h, expected to affect measurements of $H_0$. We revisit this issue of the concordance model. We find a correlation between errors in $H_0$ estimates and the density around the observer. Further, our mock observations reveal that deviations of up to 5\% can occur in Milky Way-sized halos. While this finding alone does not fully resolve the Hubble tension, it may account for part of it. It is essential to understand the limitations of N-body simulations to avoid misinterpreting data. We show that the missing power at small scales introduces errors in the root-mean-square fluctuations and in the simulated mass function. Our analytical calculation indicates that mode coupling between small and large scales depends on resolving collapsed halos. Therefore, accurate mode coupling estimates require sufficient halos in the simulation.

AI.tldr: This paper uses N-body simulations to study non-linear gravitational effects on the halo mass function (HMF), finding systematic 5-20% deviations from theoretical predictions due to cosmology and power spectrum slope. It also investigates Hubble constant ($H_0$) estimation errors correlated with local density, contributing up to 5% deviation in Milky Way-sized halos, partially addressing the Hubble tension. The study highlights limitations of N-body simulations, particularly missing small-scale power affecting RMS fluctuations and mass function accuracy, and emphasizes the need for sufficient halo resolution to capture mode coupling.
AI.motivation: Non-linear gravitational interactions influence galaxy distribution, halo abundance, and peculiar velocities, making their study essential for accurate cosmological predictions. The paper aims to understand systematic deviations in the halo mass function from theoretical models and examine how structure formation affects Hubble constant measurements.
AI.method: The authors employ N-body simulations with scale-free power spectra under an Einstein-de Sitter cosmology, and compare with $\Lambda$CDM models. They examine HMF deviations from universality, analyze the effective index correspondence, and conduct mock observations to study $H_0$ estimation errors. Analytical calculations assess mode coupling and resolution requirements.
AI.result: HMF shows 5-20% systematic deviations from theoretical predictions, with explicit dependence on the slope of the input power spectrum. An effective index of $\Lambda$CDM approximates scale-free HMF. $H_0$ errors correlate with local density; deviations up to 5% occur in Milky Way-sized halos. Missing small-scale power introduces errors in RMS fluctuations and simulated mass function. Mode coupling accuracy depends on resolving sufficient collapsed halos.
AI.conclusion: Non-linear evolution and simulation limitations must be carefully accounted for in cosmological analyses. The HMF is not universal but depends on the power spectrum slope. Local density variations can bias $H_0$ estimates, partially contributing to the Hubble tension but not fully resolving it. Adequate halo resolution is critical for accurate mode coupling estimates in N-body simulations.

title: Supermassive Black Hole Winds in X-rays: SUBWAYS IV. Tracing Radio Emission and Unveiling the Role of Winds
comment: 25 pages, to appear in A&A
summary: Most Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) are Radio Quiet, with radio emission that may arise from star-formation activity, AGN-driven winds, weak jets, and coronal activity. Disentangling these mechanisms is challenging and requires detailed multi-wavelength investigation, but it is crucial for quantifying AGN feedback in galaxy evolution. We present a detailed radio investigation of 21 X-ray selected AGN in the Supermassive Black Hole Winds in X-Rays (SUBWAYS) sample (log Lbol = 44.9-46.3 erg/s, z=0.1-0.5), selected to systematically search for Ultra-Fast Outflows (UFOs). UFOs are detected in 30% of the targets, making the sample particularly well-suited for investigating the role and signatures of multi-scale outflows at different frequencies. We build the radio SED of the sources complementing our proprietary data, collected with the JVLA at 1.5 and 6 GHz, with images from LoTSS and other publicly available radio surveys between 150 and 1400 MHz. We investigate the role and occurrence of the aforementioned mechanisms, with particular interest in outflows and their possible relation with UFOs. We combined information on spectral indices, luminosities, and morphologies of the radio emission with properties derived in other wavebands, such as Star Formation Rate, X-ray luminosity, Eddington ratio or the UFO kinetic luminosity. All the sources are detected and are mostly consistent with RQ AGN. For 80% of the sources the data suggest the presence of an outflow (wind or weak jet). Interestingly, our results indicate that AGN with UFOs tend to have larger radio extension and a steep radio spectrum consistent with outflows. Moreover, the radio emission of the 6 UFO hosts is consistent with predictions from wind-driven shock models, possibly indicating a direct connection between the two phases. Alternatively, this may reflect physical conditions favouring the rise of both phenomena.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 21 X-ray selected AGN from the SUBWAYS sample to investigate radio emission mechanisms and their connection to Ultra-Fast Outflows (UFOs). Using JVLA data and public radio surveys, they find all sources are radio-quiet AGN, with 80% showing outflow signatures. Notably, UFO hosts exhibit larger radio extensions and steeper radio spectra consistent with wind-driven shock models, suggesting a direct link between multi-scale outflows.
AI.motivation: Disentangling the origins of radio emission in Radio Quiet AGN (star formation, winds, weak jets, coronal activity) is challenging but crucial for quantifying AGN feedback in galaxy evolution.
AI.method: Radio SEDs were built using proprietary JVLA data (1.5 and 6 GHz) combined with LoTSS and other public surveys (150-1400 MHz). Multi-wavelength properties (SFR, X-ray luminosity, Eddington ratio, UFO kinetic luminosity) were correlated with radio spectral indices, luminosities, and morphologies.
AI.result: All 21 sources are detected and consistent with RQ AGN. 80% show evidence of outflows (wind or weak jet). UFO hosts tend to have larger radio extension and steeper radio spectra. The radio emission of the 6 UFO hosts aligns with wind-driven shock model predictions.
AI.conclusion: There is a possible direct connection between UFOs (detected in X-rays) and radio outflows, or alternatively, shared physical conditions that favor both phenomena.

title: Impact of Primordial Black Hole population on 21 cm observables at high redshift
comment: Submitted to A&A
summary: The 21-cm signal, one of the most promising probes of the high-redshift Universe, has traditionally been modelled without accounting for the effects of active galactic nuclei (AGN) in the pre-JWST era, primarily due to the lack of observational evidence for AGNs at z > 6. However, following the discovery of several AGNs at redshifts as high as z ~ 10 by JWST, it has become imperative to incorporate the impact of these early AGNs when predicting the 21-cm signal. Supposing that these AGNs are seeded by primordial black holes (PBHs), we study their impact with a semi-numerical model setup. Specifically, we extended the explicitly photon-conserving reionization framework, SCRIPT, including essential cosmic dawn physics and PBH contributions. This enables us to compute both the global signal and the power spectrum of the 21-cm line over the redshift range z ~ 30 - 5 within a self-consistent framework. Building on this setup, we then investigate the impact of different PBH mass functions (obeying current observational constraints) on the resulting signal. The X-ray heating from PBHs can substantially make the depth of the global 21-cm signal shallower and suppress the expected power amplitude during cosmic dawn. We also find that the choice of mass function plays a crucial role in shaping the 21-cm signal, and can, in fact, lead to significantly different predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the SCRIPT reionization framework to include primordial black holes (PBHs) as seeds for early AGNs discovered by JWST at z~10, and studies their impact on the 21-cm signal. X-ray heating from PBHs shallows the global signal and suppresses power spectrum amplitudes during cosmic dawn, with the PBH mass function significantly influencing predictions.
AI.motivation: JWST discovered AGNs at z~10, previously unaccounted for in 21-cm signal modeling. The authors aim to incorporate these early AGNs—assuming they are seeded by PBHs—into 21-cm predictions to understand their impact.
AI.method: The authors extended the SCRIPT (explicitly photon-conserving reionization) framework to include cosmic dawn physics and PBH contributions, incorporating different PBH mass functions consistent with observational constraints.
AI.result: X-ray heating from PBHs shallows the global 21-cm signal depth and suppresses power spectrum amplitude during cosmic dawn. The PBH mass function choice critically shapes the signal, yielding significantly different predictions.
AI.conclusion: Early AGNs seeded by PBHs must be accounted for in 21-cm signal modeling; the PBH mass function is a key parameter determining the observable signatures.

title: SFUMATO#: a GPU accelerated code for Self-Gravitational Radiation Hydrodynamics Simulation with Adaptive Mesh Refinement
comment: 23 pages, 23 figures, accepted for publication in PASJ
summary: We present a new implementation of the SFUMATO code, called SFUMATO#, for solving self-gravitational radiation hydrodynamics problems using adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) with the CUDA/HIP programming frameworks. The code incorporates a multigrid solver for self-gravity, radiation transfer with M1 closure and reduced speed of light approximation, non-equilibrium chemistry, thermal evolution, and sink particle schemes. We develop new non-equilibrium chemistry and thermal solvers based on a linearized implicit method, whose accuracy is validated through a series of test problems by comparison with solutions obtained using the Newton-Raphson method. By incorporating the heat capacity of dust grains, the dust temperature can be evolved without iterative energy-balance calculations. From the perspective of computational cost, we demonstrate that adopting an increased pseudo dust heat capacity accelerates the chemistry solver while preserving accuracy, even when the value is increased by up to three orders of magnitude relative to the realistic value. In addition, we perform a suite of test problems to confirm the validity of the other components of our implementation. The code supports multi-GPU execution via MPI-based parallelization. We measure the strong-scaling performance of the hydrodynamics and self-gravity solvers on both uniform and AMR grids, as well as the overall code performance using a giant molecular cloud simulation. We find that the computational cost of the self-gravity solver increases with the number of MPI processes, indicating that efficient parallel performance is achieved only when the number of devices is chosen such that the cost of the self-gravity solver remains comparable to that of the other components.

AI.tldr: SFUMATO# is a GPU-accelerated (CUDA/HIP) AMR code for self-gravitational radiation hydrodynamics, featuring multigrid gravity, M1-closure radiation transport, non-equilibrium chemistry with a linearized implicit solver, dust heat capacity treatment, and multi-GPU MPI parallelization. Performance scaling analysis shows self-gravity solver cost increases with MPI processes, requiring balanced device count for efficiency.
AI.motivation: To develop a high-performance, GPU-accelerated AMR code (SFUMATO#) that efficiently solves self-gravitational radiation hydrodynamics problems, with improved solvers for non-equilibrium chemistry and thermal evolution that avoid costly iterative calculations.
AI.method: Implemented using CUDA/HIP with AMR; multigrid solver for self-gravity; M1-closure radiation transfer with reduced speed of light approximation; linearized implicit method for non-equilibrium chemistry and thermal evolution; dust heat capacity integration to avoid iterative energy-balance; MPI-based multi-GPU parallelization.
AI.result: Increased pseudo dust heat capacity (up to 3 orders of magnitude) accelerates chemistry solver while preserving accuracy; self-gravity solver cost scales with MPI process count; efficient parallel performance requires balancing self-gravity cost with other components.
AI.conclusion: SFUMATO# is a validated, GPU-accelerated AMR radiation-hydrodynamics code; optimal multi-GPU performance depends on choosing device count where self-gravity solver cost remains comparable to other code components.

title: Saturation Mechanisms in the Interacting Dark Sector
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures
summary: We introduce a family of phenomenological cosmological models featuring an interacting dark sector modulated by a sparseness scale parameter, in order to describe the late-time accelerated expansion of the universe. The sparseness scale, inspired by well-established saturation mechanisms in ecology and biology, is introduced in the interaction as a half-saturation constant that bounds the energy exchange between dark matter and dark energy, controls the dynamical behaviour of the physical variables and can prevent the phantom crossing. We consider three nonlinear interacting models, where two of them recover the linear interacting scenarios when the sparsity parameter vanishes. We examine the phase-space of the cosmological field equations by using the Hubble normalization approach. We determine the stationary points and their stability properties in order to reconstruct the asymptotics behaviour of the field equations. Such an analysis allows us to demonstrate the effects of the sparseness scale on the background dynamics. We test the interacting models with observational data. Specifically, we employ Supernovae catalogues, cosmic chronometers, Baryon Acoustic Oscillation measurements from DESI DR2, and redshift-space distortion measurements of the growth of large-scale structure through the $f$ and $fσ_8$ observables. The Bayesian analysis suggests that, for two of the three models, a vanishing sparsity parameter is disfavoured at more than the 95\% confidence interval, providing observational support for a nonzero sparseness scale in the dark sector interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a family of dark sector interaction models with a sparseness scale parameter (inspired by ecology/biology saturation mechanisms) that bounds energy exchange between dark matter and dark energy. Using phase-space analysis and observational data (Supernovae, cosmic chronometers, DESI DR2 BAO, and redshift-space distortions), they find that for two of three models, a nonzero sparseness scale is favored at >95% confidence, preventing phantom crossing and stabilizing the dynamics.
AI.motivation: To address late-time cosmic acceleration by introducing a phenomenological dark sector interaction model where a sparseness scale parameter, inspired by saturation mechanisms in ecology/biology, regulates energy exchange between dark matter and dark energy, preventing phantom crossing and unbounded behavior.
AI.method: Three nonlinear interacting dark sector models were constructed, with a half-saturation sparseness parameter modulating the interaction. Two models recover linear interactions when sparsity vanishes. Phase-space analysis employed Hubble normalization to find stationary points and assess stability. Bayesian model selection used observational data: Supernovae, cosmic chronometers, DESI DR2 BAO, and fσ8 redshift-space distortion measurements.
AI.result: For two of the three models, a vanishing sparseness parameter is disfavored at more than 95% confidence interval, providing strong observational evidence for a nonzero sparseness scale in the dark sector interaction.
AI.conclusion: The sparseness scale is an observationally supported feature that bounds dark sector interactions, prevents phantom crossing, and improves agreement with cosmological data, suggesting that nonlinear saturation effects may be relevant in dark sector phenomenology.

title: Signatures of Very Massive Stars in the Epoch of Reionization
comment: Submitted to A&A Letters, 4 pages and 2 Figures (+Appendix)
summary: We present ultra-deep ($\simeq 20-30$ hours), rest-frame UV spectroscopy with NIRSpec/JWST of two UV-bright galaxies at $z\sim 8.7$, CEERS-1019 and CEERS-1025 ($Z_{\rm neb} \simeq 0.1 Z_{\odot}$). The spectra reveal exceptionally strong P-Cygni profiles in wind lines (NV $λ$1240 and CIV $λ$1550) and significant broad and strong HeII $λ$1640 emission ($\rm EW\simeq 2-4$ A). We compare the observations with synthetic stellar population models at $Z_{\star} \simeq 0.1 Z_{\odot}$, both including and excluding very massive stars (VMS). Models including VMS provide a markedly improved fit to the data relative to non-VMS models ($Δ$AIC and $Δ$BIC $> 70$), which fail to reproduce the observed strengths of the wind features. A comparison with empirical spectra of VMS-dominated systems in the local Universe further supports this interpretation. The best-fit VMS models imply extremely young ages of the stellar populations ($\simeq 1.5-2.0$Myr) and high ionizing photon production efficiencies ($\log ξ_{\rm ion} [\rm Hz erg^{-1}] \gtrsim 25.8$), exceeding those inferred from non-VMS models by $\sim 0.1-0.2$ dex. These results provide evidence for an overabundance of VMS at high-$z$ with an IMF extending well beyond $100 M_{\odot}$, and highlight their potential role in shaping the rest-frame UV spectra, chemical enrichment, and ionizing output of galaxies in the early Universe.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRSpec ultra-deep UV spectroscopy of two z~8.7 galaxies (CEERS-1019, CEERS-1025) reveals strong P-Cygni wind profiles (NV λ1240, CIV λ1550) and broad HeII λ1640 emission. Comparison with synthetic models shows that including very massive stars (VMS) provides a significantly better fit than non-VMS models, implying extremely young stellar populations (~1.5-2.0 Myr) and high ionizing photon production efficiencies, suggesting an overabundance of VMS with an IMF extending beyond 100 M☉ in the early Universe.
AI.motivation: To investigate the presence and role of very massive stars (VMS) in the early Universe by obtaining and analyzing ultra-deep rest-frame UV spectra of high-redshift galaxies, testing whether standard stellar population models can explain the observed spectral features.
AI.method: Ultra-deep (~20-30 hours) rest-frame UV spectroscopy using NIRSpec/JWST of two UV-bright galaxies at z~8.7. The observed spectra were compared with synthetic stellar population models at Z⋆~0.1 Z☉, both including and excluding very massive stars, using AIC/BIC model selection criteria and empirical comparisons with local VMS-dominated systems.
AI.result: Models including VMS provide a markedly improved fit (ΔAIC and ΔBIC > 70) compared to non-VMS models. Best-fit VMS models imply extremely young ages (~1.5-2.0 Myr) and high log ξion ≳ 25.8 Hz erg⁻¹, exceeding non-VMS models by ~0.1-0.2 dex. Strong P-Cygni wind profiles and broad HeII emission are observed.
AI.conclusion: The results provide evidence for an overabundance of very massive stars at high redshift with an IMF extending well beyond 100 M☉, highlighting their potential role in shaping rest-frame UV spectra, chemical enrichment, and ionizing output of galaxies in the early Universe.

title: SPURS: Bursty Star Formation in an Extremely Luminous Weak Emission Line Galaxy at $z=9.3$
comment: 35 pages, 19 figures, 3 tables. Comments welcome!
summary: JWST has revealed a population of super-luminous early galaxies with a volume density in excess of most expectations. The spectra reveal diverse properties: while some reveal strong emission lines characteristic of galaxies in the midst of strong bursts, others show weak emission lines that could reflect old stellar populations, large escape fractions, or post-burst star formation histories. Through the JWST Cycle 4 large program SPURS, we have obtained ultra-deep (29 hr) rest-frame UV spectroscopy of a z=9.3 super-luminous ($M_{\rm UV}=-21.66$) galaxy with large assembled stellar mass (1.6$\times$10$^9$ $M_\odot$) and extremely weak emission lines (H$β$ EW $\approx25$~Å). The strong stellar wind features and rest-optical line ratios suggest the galaxy is already significantly enriched, with a metallicity of 0.4--0.7~Z$_\odot$. The interstellar absorption lines reveal outflows ($v\simeq -161$~km~s$^{-1}$) with a large neutral gas covering fraction, suggesting that the weak emission lines are not due to large escape fractions. The combination of the Balmer break, weak emission lines, and stellar wind features constrains the star formation history, indicating a recent burst of star formation lasting 10--20 Myr followed by a downturn over the last 10~Myr. The observations suggest that $z\gtrsim 9$ weak emission line galaxies such as this source can be explained by stochastic star formation, provided that the downturns in star formation are recent (i.e., <10 Myr prior to observation). The ultra-deep grating spectrum enables the IGM damping wing to be characterized, decoupling the effects of local absorption. The smooth Ly$α$ break indicates that this source, one of the most massive galaxies known at z>9, is likely situated in a small ionized bubble ($0.29_{-0.09}^{+0.11}$~pMpc), as is common at large neutral hydrogen fractions ($\bar{x}_{\rm HI}=0.81_{-0.21}^{+0.14}$).

AI.tldr: JWST ultra-deep spectroscopy of a z=9.3 super-luminous galaxy (SPURS program) reveals weak emission lines, high metallicity (0.4-0.7 Z⊙), recent burst followed by downturn in star formation, strong outflows with high neutral gas covering fraction, and a small ionized bubble (0.29 pMpc) in a largely neutral IGM (x_HI=0.81).
AI.motivation: JWST has discovered an unexpectedly high volume density of super-luminous early galaxies, with diverse spectral properties that challenge existing models. Some show strong emission lines, while others exhibit weak emission lines that could reflect old stellar populations, large escape fractions, or post-burst star formation histories - understanding these diverse populations is crucial.
AI.method: Ultra-deep (29 hr) rest-frame UV spectroscopy from JWST Cycle 4 SPURS large program on a z=9.3 super-luminous galaxy (M_UV=-21.66, stellar mass 1.6×10^9 M⊙). Analysis of stellar wind features, rest-optical line ratios, interstellar absorption lines, Balmer break, and IGM damping wing characterization.
AI.result: Metallicity 0.4-0.7 Z⊙; outflows at v=-161 km/s with high neutral gas covering fraction (ruling out large escape fractions as cause of weak lines); recent burst lasting 10-20 Myr followed by downturn over last 10 Myr; small ionized bubble of 0.29 pMpc in highly neutral IGM (x_HI=0.81).
AI.conclusion: Weak emission line galaxies at z≳9 can be explained by stochastic star formation with recent (within 10 Myr) downturns. The galaxy resides in a small ionized bubble as expected at large neutral hydrogen fractions, demonstrating that ultra-deep spectroscopy can decouple local absorption from IGM damping wing effects.

title: An Old, Low-mass, Metal-poor Hypervelocity Star Candidate Consistent with a Galactic Center Origin
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables, Accepted for publication in ApJL
summary: We report the discovery of DESI-HVS1, a hypervelocity star (HVS) candidate identified from DESI DR1 spectroscopy and Gaia DR3 astrometry. DESI-HVS1 is an old, low-mass, metal-poor F-type star with a mass of $0.8\,M_\odot$, an age of $\sim14.1$~Gyr, and $\mathrm{[Fe/H]}=-1.6$. It is located at a heliocentric distance of $3.77^{+0.39}_{-0.36}$~kpc and has a Galactocentric total velocity of $523^{+46}_{-47}\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, marginally exceeding the local escape speed, corresponding to an unbound probability of $P_{\rm ub} \sim 50\%$. Backward orbit integrations show that DESI-HVS1 had a closest approach to the Galactic Centre (GC) of $0.40^{+0.23}_{-0.11}\,\mathrm{kpc}$, with a velocity of $682^{+22}_{-35}\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and a flight time of $12.89^{+0.92}_{-0.74}\,\mathrm{Myr}$. The reconstructed orbit exhibits a clear perigalactic turning point and only a single crossing of the Galactic midplane ($P_{\rm cross} > 0.95$). These properties suggest that DESI-HVS1 is most naturally explained by the Hills mechanism, although alternative scenarios cannot be entirely ruled out. Its discovery provides the first strong evidence for an old, low-mass HVS candidate consistent with a GC origin, indicating that the apparent dominance of young, massive GC-origin HVSs is likely a consequence of observational selection effects.

AI.tldr: DESI-HVS1 is a hypervelocity star candidate discovered from DESI DR1 and Gaia DR3 data. It is an old (14.1 Gyr), low-mass (0.8 M☉), metal-poor ([Fe/H]=-1.6) F-type star with a Galactocentric velocity of ~523 km/s, marginally exceeding the local escape speed. Orbit analysis suggests a Galactic Center origin via the Hills mechanism, with a closest approach of 0.40 kpc to the GC and a flight time of ~12.9 Myr. This is the first strong evidence for an old, low-mass HVS from the GC, implying that observational biases previously favored young, massive HVSs.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize hypervelocity stars (HVSs) ejected from the Galactic Center, particularly old, low-mass ones that are rarely observed, in order to understand the full population of HVSs and test whether observational selection effects have biased previous detections toward young, massive stars.
AI.method: Combined DESI DR1 spectroscopy with Gaia DR3 astrometry to identify the HVS candidate. Performed stellar parameter fitting (mass, age, metallicity), distance estimation, velocity calculation, and backward orbit integrations to trace the star's origin and dynamics, including perigalactic approach and Galactic midplane crossing analysis.
AI.result: DESI-HVS1 has a mass of 0.8 M☉, age ~14.1 Gyr, [Fe/H] = -1.6, heliocentric distance ~3.77 kpc, Galactocentric velocity ~523 km/s, unbound probability ~50%. Orbit shows closest GC approach of 0.40 kpc at ~682 km/s, flight time ~12.9 Myr, single midplane crossing (P > 0.95), consistent with the Hills mechanism.
AI.conclusion: DESI-HVS1 is the first robust old, low-mass HVS candidate consistent with a Galactic Center origin via the Hills mechanism. Its discovery suggests that the observed dominance of young, massive HVSs from the GC is due to observational selection effects, implying a more diverse population of ejected stars exists.

title: Massive star formation at the Galactic crossroads: Insights from G358.69+0.03 in the Galactic center
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 14+11 pages, 18 figures
summary: We investigated the high-mass star formation activity in a subregion of the Sagittarius E star-forming complex, centered at (l,b) = (358.69 deg, 0.03 deg), where infrared and radio sources trace a prominent U-shaped structure that has not been identified in previous studies. We used radio continuum data from the Global View on Star Formation (GLOSTAR) survey, which is a wide-band radio (4-8 GHz) survey of the Milky Way that combines data from the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array and the Effelsberg 100 m telescope. Using BLOBCAT source extraction software, we identified 49 compact radio sources. Based on multiwavelength associations and spectral index estimates, we identified GLOSTAR counterparts to 27 previously confirmed HII regions, detected radio emission from 3 WISE "radio-quiet" candidates, and report 5 new HII region candidates. The derived physical properties indicate that most are relatively evolved HII regions. We find around 50 cold dust clumps, predominantly toward the south and southeast. Mid-infrared flux-ratio maps ([4.5]/[3.6]) show localized shock enhancements along the arc and adjacent clumps, and 15 clumps exhibit SiO emission with broad components indicative of shocks. Together with CO data, the SiO velocity components delineate a continuous (>100 km/s) velocity bridge that links the far dust-lane inflow to the central molecular zone (CMZ) stream. The largest concentration of clumps and compact HII regions lies at this interface. These combined diagnostics favor a scenario in which bar-driven cloud-cloud collision at the far dust-lane-CMZ interface compressed the gas and triggered the observed high-mass star formation.

AI.tldr: This study investigates high-mass star formation in a subregion of the Sagittarius E complex (l,b = 358.69°, 0.03°), using multiwavelength data from GLOSTAR, Spitzer/IRAC, and molecular line observations. 49 compact radio sources were identified, including 27 known HII regions, 3 WISE "radio-quiet" candidates, and 5 new candidates. Physical properties suggest mostly evolved HII regions. SiO observations reveal broad components and a >100 km/s velocity bridge linking the far dust-lane inflow to the CMZ stream. The evidence supports bar-driven cloud-cloud collision at the far dust-lane-CMZ interface as the trigger for high-mass star formation.
AI.motivation: To understand the high-mass star formation activity in a previously unidentified U-shaped structure in the Sagittarius E complex and identify the triggering mechanism for star formation at the interface between the far dust lane and the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of the Milky Way.
AI.method: Radio continuum data from GLOSTAR (4-8 GHz, VLA+Effelsberg), BLOBCAT source extraction, multiwavelength associations, spectral index analysis, mid-infrared [4.5]/[3.6] flux-ratio mapping, CO and SiO molecular line observations.
AI.result: 49 compact radio sources identified (27 known HII regions, 3 WISE "radio-quiet" candidates, 5 new HII region candidates). ~50 cold dust clumps found. SiO broad components indicate shocks. A continuous >100 km/s velocity bridge links far dust-lane inflow to CMZ stream. Largest concentration of clumps and HII regions at the interface.
AI.conclusion: Bar-driven cloud-cloud collision at the far dust-lane-CMZ interface compressed gas and triggered the observed high-mass star formation.
